summary: Specifies procedures for using bidirectional tunnels as provider tunnels in multicast VPNs for BGP/MPLS IP VPNs, extending earlier procedures for carrying customer multicast data through a provider backbone.

eli5.summary: One shared two-way pipe carries many customers' group broadcasts instead of building separate pipes.

questions: what is the pmsi tunnel attribute
subtitle: The missing rules for carrying customer multicast across a provider backbone on two-way tunnels.

tldr.problem: The base multicast VPN specifications let a BGP attribute name a bidirectional tunnel, but they leave out the procedures for actually using one: which customer flows go on which tunnel, how that is advertised and how receivers know where to expect a flow.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7582 defines three ways to instantiate a PMSI with bidirectional tunnels (Flat Partitioned, Hierarchical Partitioned and Unpartitioned), plus matching rules for transmission and reception and a new 'all BIDIR-PIM groups' wildcard.
tldr.outcome: It updates RFC 6513, RFC 6514 and RFC 6625, and has itself been updated by RFC 8534 and RFC 9573. Supporting bidirectional P-tunnels is optional, but an implementation that does must meet a stated minimal feature set.

today: RFC 7582 is a Proposed Standard from July 2015. It is updated by RFC 8534 and RFC 9573, and it has not been obsoleted. It updates RFC 6513, RFC 6514 and RFC 6625.

sections.title: The Gap in the Base MVPN Specifications
sections.content:
The specifications for multicast in BGP/MPLS IP VPNs (RFC 6513, RFC 6514 and RFC 6625) let customer multicast data cross a service provider's network through a set of multicast tunnels. The tunnels are advertised in BGP auto-discovery (A-D) routes using the Provider Multicast Service Interface (PMSI) Tunnel attribute, or PTA.

Those documents allow bidirectional (multipoint-to-multipoint) distribution trees and say how to encode their identifiers in the PTA. They declared the full procedures for using such trees to be out of scope. RFC 7582 supplies them: how customer flows are assigned to specific bidirectional tunnels, how that is advertised, and how a receiver works out which tunnel a flow should arrive on.

No new data encapsulation is defined. Section 12 of RFC 6513 applies unchanged. Where this document conflicts with RFC 6513, RFC 6514 or RFC 6625 on using bidirectional P-tunnels to instantiate PMSIs, this document takes precedence.

The RFC uses the prefixes C- (customer address space) and P- (provider address space). A C-flow is a customer multicast flow, written (C-S,C-G) for a source and group. A P-tunnel is a tunnel through the provider network, here always a bidirectional multicast distribution tree: traffic may enter at any node and travel both toward and away from the root.

A PMSI is a conceptual overlay that lets one provider edge (PE) router multicast to the other PEs of a VPN, and P-tunnels instantiate it. An I-PMSI (inclusive) reaches all PEs in the MVPN. An S-PMSI (selective) reaches some of them, and is advertised by an S-PMSI A-D route. Wildcards such as (C-*,C-G) and (C-*,C-*) let one route cover many flows.

A C-BIDIR flow is a customer flow whose tree is built by BIDIR-PIM. Such groups have a Rendezvous Point Address (RPA), written C-RPA in the customer space and P-RPA in the provider space.
sections.eli5:
The old rulebook said a shared two-way pipe was allowed but never explained how to use it. This new rulebook fills in the missing instructions.

A flow is one conversation of group messages. A PMSI is like a group chat among the provider's routers: everyone in the chat, or only some of them.

sections.title: Two Tunnel Technologies and Three Instantiation Methods
sections.content:
Two bidirectional tunnel technologies are supported: multipoint-to-multipoint LSPs (MP2MP LSPs) made with the LDP extensions of RFC 6388, and trees made with BIDIR-PIM (RFC 5015). Others are out of scope.

Why use them? One reason is to give customers C-BIDIR support using the Partitioned Set of PEs technique. The other is to save state in transit nodes: if an MVPN has n PEs with sources, unidirectional trees need n trees, one rooted at each, while a single bidirectional tree can serve all of them.

Three PMSI instantiation methods are defined, and all PEs of an MVPN must be provisioned with the same one:

  • Flat Partitioned: several bidirectional P-tunnels, each with one distinguished PE, which is the root. No upstream-assigned labels are needed.
  • Hierarchical Partitioned: the same, but the P-tunnels are aggregated as inner tunnels inside one outer tunnel using PE Distinguisher Labels. It needs upstream-assigned MPLS labels.
  • Unpartitioned: a PMSI can be instantiated by a single bidirectional P-tunnel. Receivers cannot tell which PE sent a packet.

It is valid to use the Unpartitioned Method for I-PMSIs and a Partitioned Method for S-PMSIs, and to mix unidirectional and bidirectional P-tunnels for different S-PMSIs.
sections.eli5: There are three ways to run the shared bus. One uses several buses, each with its own captain. One packs those buses inside a bigger bus. One uses a single bus where nobody can tell who got on first.

sections.title: The All BIDIR-PIM Wildcard
sections.content:
RFC 6625 allows the source or group in a BGP route to be a wildcard. RFC 7582 adds a special group wildcard meaning all BIDIR-PIM groups, written (C-*,C-*-BIDIR). A route carrying it says: by default, all BIDIR-PIM customer traffic in this VPN that is not bound to another P-tunnel uses the tunnel named in this route's PTA.

The encoding is a group field 8 bits long whose value is zero. The "multicast group length" field holds 0x08 and the "multicast group" field is the single octet 0x00. This is distinct from the wildcard encoding in RFC 6625. It is useful when one bidirectional tunnel carries the C-BIDIR flows while unidirectional tunnels carry everything else.
sections.eli5: It is a sticker that says "every two-way group goes on this bus unless told otherwise."

sections.title: Tunnel-Specific Procedures
sections.content:
A bidirectional P-tunnel may be advertised in the PTA of an Intra-AS I-PMSI A-D route or an S-PMSI A-D route. Advertising one in an Inter-AS I-PMSI A-D route is out of scope.

A BIDIR-PIM P-tunnel is identified by a unique P-group address, which maps to a single P-RPA in the provider's address space. PEs build the tunnel by sending PIM Join/Prune messages toward the P-RPA. The RFC recommends that the path from each PE to the RPA consist entirely of point-to-point links, which makes the Designated Forwarder Election quick and simple. Hierarchical Partitioning over BIDIR-PIM is out of scope, so the originator SHOULD NOT include a PE Distinguisher Labels attribute, and if one is present it MUST be ignored for the data plane.

An MP2MP LSP is identified by an MP2MP FEC element: the root node's IP address plus an opaque value unique within that root. An implementation SHOULD be able to accept and process a PTA using any legal tunnel identifier type, even if it does not advertise every type.
sections.eli5: Each bus line has a name tag: a group address for one kind, or a root address plus a number for the other. Everyone who rides must know the tag.

sections.title: Flat and Hierarchical Partitioning
sections.content:
With either Partitioned Method used for C-BIDIR support, a C-BIDIR flow MUST be carried only on an I-PMSI or on a (C-*,C-G-BIDIR), (C-*,C-*-BIDIR) or (C-*,C-*) S-PMSI. A PE MUST NOT originate any (C-S,C-G-BIDIR) S-PMSI A-D routes.

In Flat Partitioning the originating PE MUST be the root of the P-tunnel in its PTA, so no two PEs can advertise the same tunnel. A receiver treats the root of the arrival tunnel as the packet's distinguished PE. For a unidirectional flow that is the sender. For a bidirectional flow it is the sender's upstream PE for the flow's C-RPA. A packet whose distinguished PE is not the expected one MUST be discarded, which prevents duplicate data.

In Hierarchical Partitioning, only MP2MP LSPs are covered. The tunnel in the PTA is the outer tunnel, and the distinguished PE is identified by a PE Distinguisher Label deeper in the label stack. Labels are allocated and advertised by the root node of the outer LSP, each IP address and each label may appear at most once in the attribute, and otherwise the attribute is malformed and treat-as-withdraw error handling MUST be used. Packets arriving with unexpected values of the top two labels MUST be discarded.

Hierarchical Partitioning gives the same function as Flat Partitioning with less state in the core, but needs upstream-assigned labels that not all hardware supports.
sections.eli5: Every packet has to be traced back to the right captain. If a packet shows up from the wrong captain's bus, it gets thrown away so nobody gets two copies.

sections.title: Choosing the Tunnel: Match for Transmission and Reception
sections.content:
A PE needing to send a C-BIDIR flow tries routes in order of specificity. If the C-RPA is local or reached through a VRF interface, it uses a route it originated itself. Otherwise it uses a route installed from the upstream PE for the C-RPA. In both cases the order is (C-*,C-G-BIDIR), then (C-*,C-*-BIDIR), then (C-*,C-*). If none matches an S-PMSI, the flow goes on the I-PMSI; if no I-PMSI route meets the conditions, the flow MUST NOT be transmitted.

Reception mirrors this. The receiver finds the upstream PE for the C-RPA, treats it as the distinguished PE, and looks for the same sequence of routes from that PE. In the Hierarchical case a flow may also match a route from the root of an MP2MP LSP if that root's route carries a PE Distinguisher Labels attribute assigning a label to the upstream PE.
sections.eli5: A router checks the most specific sign first, then a more general one, then the catch-all. It sends and listens on whichever bus the first matching sign names.

sections.title: The Unpartitioned Method and Compliance
sections.content:
In the Unpartitioned Method, at least one VRF of the MVPN MUST originate an Intra-AS I-PMSI A-D route with a PTA naming a bidirectional P-tunnel. Other routes may omit the PTA, but any PTA present MUST name a bidirectional tunnel. A PE SHOULD transmit on its own advertised tunnel but MAY use any advertised tunnel. Receivers treat all of them as the same I-PMSI, and the disposition of a packet MUST NOT depend on which tunnel it arrived on. Several tunnels add robustness but no functionality.

Because receivers cannot associate packets with a distinguished PE, duplicate detection by the technique of Section 9.1.1 of RFC 6513 is not possible, and the Partitioned Set of PEs technique cannot be supported. C-BIDIR traffic would have to ride an S-PMSI built with a Partitioned Method.

Compliance: implementing bidirectional P-tunnels is OPTIONAL. An implementation that does MUST support at least one of the two tunnel technologies. A PE without Partitioned Set support is compliant if it supports the Unpartitioned Method. A PE with that support MUST at minimum carry all of a VPN's C-BIDIR traffic on a (C-*,C-*-BIDIR) S-PMSI using the Flat Partitioned Method.
sections.eli5: With one big shared bus, nobody can tell who boarded first, so some tricks for spotting duplicates stop working. The rules say how to cope and what the minimum a vendor must do.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC adds nothing here. It states that there are no additional security considerations beyond those of RFC 6513 and RFC 6514, or any that may apply to the protocol used to set up the bidirectional tunnels (RFC 5015 and RFC 6388).
sections.eli5: It says: no new dangers beyond the ones already known for the old rulebooks and the tunnel-building tools.
